rationale: Art. 72 requires providers to collect and analyse performance data from deployed high-risk systems to evaluate continuous compliance, and Art. 26(5) requires deployers to monitor operation and suspend use when they identify a risk. Anomaly Detection supplies the statistical and model-based detection of unusual system, data, or AI behaviour that makes those monitoring duties effective; the Act does not prescribe detection methods, so alignment is partial.

Art. 72 requires a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the AI technology and risks, Art. 26(5) requires deployers to monitor operation per the instructions for use, and Art. 12 requires automatic logging over the system lifetime. Continuous Monitoring provides the automated, continuous monitoring of security, privacy, and model performance that these provisions depend on.

Art. 73 requires reporting of serious incidents to market surveillance authorities within defined time limits, Art. 20 requires corrective actions and withdrawal or recall when a system is non-conforming, and Art. 26(5) requires deployers to inform the provider and authorities of risks and serious incidents. Incident Management provides the identification, containment, analysis, and recovery capability these duties rely on.

Art. 25 allocates obligations along the AI value chain and requires written agreements and information from suppliers of systems, tools, and components, and Art. 26(5) requires deployers to monitor systems obtained from providers. Monitor Third Parties supplies the ongoing oversight of providers and suppliers that keeps those arrangements effective. Partial alignment: the Act sets obligations rather than a monitoring programme.

Art. 17(1)(l) and (m) require the quality management system to cover resource management and an accountability framework that sets out management responsibilities. Top Management Commitment provides the visible leadership direction and resourcing that the accountability framework assigns to management.

Art. 17(1)(m) requires an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and staff for all aspects of the QMS. Charters & Committees establishes the formal oversight bodies through which those responsibilities are discharged. Partial alignment: the Act requires the framework, not a committee structure.

Art. 16 places the obligations for high-risk AI on the provider as an organisation, and Art. 17(1)(m) requires an accountability framework that reaches management. Executive Leadership & Board Oversight provides the governing-body oversight of compliance and risk posture that discharges those organisational obligations.

Art. 14 requires high-risk systems to be designed for effective oversight by natural persons who can understand, monitor, override, and stop the system, Art. 26(2) requires deployers to assign oversight to competent, trained persons with authority, and Art. 17(1)(m) requires an accountability framework. Accountability ensures every AI decision has a traceable human owner with authority to act.

Art. 10(2)(f) and (g) require examination of possible biases in datasets and measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate them, and Art. 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment that covers discrimination risk. Fairness adopts quantitative fairness metrics and enforces mitigation when disparities exceed thresholds.

Art. 10(4) requires datasets to take account of the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural, or functional setting in which the system is intended to be used. Cultural Considerations requires contextual review and jurisdiction-aware labelling and UX before deployments. Partial alignment: the Act addresses data representativeness, not cultural review as such.

Art. 13 requires high-risk systems to be designed for transparency with instructions for use, Art. 50 requires disclosure when people interact with AI or receive AI-generated content, and Art. 86 gives affected persons a right to an explanation of individual decisions. Transparency publishes explainability statements and disclosures of AI use that satisfy these duties.

Art. 5 prohibits specified AI practices, Art. 26(1) requires deployers to use high-risk systems in accordance with the instructions for use, and Art. 4 requires staff AI literacy. COC: Acceptable Use translates these limits into rules that personnel follow for use of AI systems and data.

Art. 95 encourages voluntary codes of conduct applying the ethical principles for trustworthy AI (human agency, fairness, transparency, accountability) to non-high-risk systems, and Recital 27 sets out those principles. COC: Ethical Principles for AI & Tech operationalises the same principles. Partial alignment: the Act makes this voluntary.

Art. 17(1)(a) requires the QMS to include a strategy for regulatory compliance, and Art. 17(1)(m) an accountability framework, both in documented policies, procedures, and instructions. Core Policies provides the governed suite of policies across security, privacy, AI, ethics, and resilience that the QMS documentation consists of.

Art. 15(5) requires high-risk systems to be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter use, outputs, or performance, and Art. 17 requires that compliance be governed by documented policy. Security Policies sets the enforceable information-security expectations that implement this.

Art. 15(4) requires technical redundancy, backup, and fail-safe plans, Art. 17(1)(i) requires procedures for serious incident reporting, and Art. 20 requires corrective action when a system is non-conforming. Response & Resilience Policies establishes the incident response, continuity, and recovery policies that implement these duties.

Art. 17(1) requires a documented quality management system covering compliance strategy, design and development techniques, data management, risk management, monitoring, and accountability for high-risk AI. AI Policies codifies the principles for responsible, secure, and ethical AI design, deployment, and operation that this QMS documentation expresses.

Art. 10(5) permits processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection only under strict safeguards (necessity, security, access limits, deletion), Art. 2(7) preserves the application of EU data protection law, and Art. 59 sets conditions for personal data use in sandboxes. Privacy Policies defines the rules for lawful processing of personal and sensitive data in AI.

Art. 17(1)(m) requires the accountability framework to set out staff responsibilities, Art. 4 requires providers and deployers to ensure AI literacy of staff, and Art. 26(2) requires oversight staff to have competence, training, and authority. HR Policies supports these through role definition and training expectations. Partial alignment: the Act does not address the employee lifecycle.

Art. 25 sets responsibilities along the AI value chain, including written agreements with suppliers of systems, tools, services, components, or processes, and Art. 17(1)(l) requires security-of-supply measures. Supply-Chain Policies sets the security, privacy, and ethical standards suppliers and partners must meet over the contract lifecycle.

Art. 10 requires training, validation, and testing datasets to be subject to data governance practices covering design choices, collection, preparation, assumptions, availability and suitability, bias examination, and gaps, and Art. 17(1)(f) requires systems and procedures for data management. Data-Governance Policies sets the rules for data quality, integrity, lifecycle, and responsible use.

Art. 17(1)(b) to (e) require the QMS to define techniques, procedures, and systematic actions for design, development, quality control, testing, and the technical specifications and standards applied, and Art. 40 gives a presumption of conformity for harmonised standards. Core Standards turns policy commitments into the measurable, auditable standards those clauses call for.

Art. 15(5) requires technical solutions to address AI-specific vulnerabilities such as data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, and confidentiality attacks, and Art. 42(2) presumes compliance for systems certified under the Cyber Resilience Act. Security Standards defines the technical and procedural standards, including AI-specific security requirements, that implement this.

Art. 15(4) requires robustness through redundancy, backup, and fail-safe plans, and Art. 17(1)(i) and Art. 73 require procedures for handling and reporting serious incidents. Response & Resilience Standards sets the standardised processes and criteria for incident response, disaster recovery, and continuity, including AI failure modes.

Art. 17(1)(b) to (f) require documented techniques and procedures for design, development, verification, testing, validation, and data management, and Art. 40 and 41 provide harmonised standards and common specifications. AI Standards translates AI policy into measurable standards governing data, model development and testing, deployment, monitoring, and retirement.

Art. 10(5) sets conditions for processing special categories of personal data for bias detection, Art. 2(7) preserves GDPR obligations, and Art. 27(4) allows a FRIA to build on an existing DPIA. Data Privacy Compliance provides the demonstrable accountability for data protection law that these provisions presume.

Art. 53(1)(c) requires general-purpose AI providers to adopt a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including rights reservations, and Art. 53(1)(d) a public summary of training content; Art. 78 requires confidentiality of trade secrets obtained by authorities. Intellectual Property Management protects proprietary data, code, and models while respecting third-party rights.

Art. 16 lists provider obligations for high-risk AI (compliance with Section 2, QMS, documentation, logs, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration, corrective action, cooperation), Art. 26 lists deployer obligations, Art. 49 requires registration in the EU database, and Art. 47 the declaration of conformity. AI Regulatory Compliance ensures AI systems conform to these obligations.

Art. 15(5) requires an appropriate level of cybersecurity for high-risk systems, and Art. 42(2) links that requirement to certification under the Cyber Resilience Act. Cybersecurity Regulatory Compliance aligns cybersecurity controls with these legal obligations and maintains continuous compliance.

Art. 5(1)(c) prohibits social scoring that leads to detrimental or disproportionate treatment, Art. 10(2)(f) and (g) require bias examination and mitigation in datasets, and Art. 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment before deploying certain high-risk systems. Ethical Use, Fairness & Bias Compliance ensures AI practices are fair, transparent, and non-discriminatory.

Art. 10(5) requires documented safeguards, access controls, and deletion for special-category data used in bias detection, Art. 27 requires impact assessment of effects on fundamental rights including privacy, and Art. 59 governs personal data in sandboxes. Privacy Program provides the enterprise-wide programme that manages personal data lawfully across AI activities.

Art. 9 requires a risk management system that is a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the lifecycle, and Art. 17(1)(g) requires the QMS to include that system. Risk Management Framework establishes the unified enterprise risk framework that integrates AI, security, privacy, and operational risk under one process.

Art. 9(5) requires that residual risk associated with each hazard and the overall residual risk be judged acceptable, and Art. 9(3) limits the system to risks that may be reasonably mitigated. Risk Appetite and Tolerance defines and approves the thresholds against which that acceptability judgement is made.

Art. 9(2) requires identification and analysis of known and foreseeable risks, estimation of risks from intended use and foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market data, and adoption of risk management measures, and Art. 55(1)(b) requires systemic-risk assessment and mitigation for GPAI. Risk Management Program: AI operationalises exactly this lifecycle programme.

Art. 15(5) requires an appropriate level of cybersecurity in light of the risks, with technical solutions tailored to the circumstances, and Art. 9(2) requires those risks to be identified and treated. Risk-Management Program: Cybersecurity identifies, analyses, and mitigates cyber risk against threat intelligence and business impact.

Art. 25 allocates responsibilities along the value chain and requires written agreements and information from suppliers, and Art. 17(1)(l) requires security-of-supply measures. Risk-Management Program: Third-Party identifies and manages the risks vendors and partners pose to data, systems, and AI integrity.

Art. 11 and Annex IV require technical documentation describing the system's intended purpose, interaction with hardware and software, versions, forms of placing on the market, and the hardware on which it runs. System Boundaries establishes the precise technical and physical boundaries and interfaces that this documentation describes.

Art. 9(2) requires risks to be assessed against the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and Annex IV requires the intended purpose and context to be documented. Goals & Context evaluates internal and external context and stakeholder expectations to set risk-informed governance goals. Partial alignment: the Act addresses system context, not organisational goal setting.

Art. 6 and Annex III determine which systems are high-risk, Art. 49 requires registration of high-risk systems and of systems a provider concludes are not high-risk, and Art. 51 classifies GPAI with systemic risk. AI Scope identifies all AI systems under organisational control, categorises them by risk, and declares lifecycle coverage.

Art. 15 requires an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity proportionate to the risks of each high-risk system. Security Scope determines which assets and environments the security programme protects and how protection is proportionate to criticality. Partial alignment: the Act scopes by system risk, not by security programme.

Art. 2 defines who and what the Regulation applies to, Art. 6 defines high-risk classification, and Art. 17(1)(a) requires a strategy for regulatory compliance including conformity assessment procedures. Regulatory Scope determines the applicable legal, contractual, and customer requirements the management system must address.

Art. 25 requires providers to specify by written agreement the information, capabilities, access, and assistance that suppliers of components must give, and Art. 26(5) requires deployers to monitor and report on systems obtained from providers. Third-Party Risk Management assesses vendors and partners and writes these requirements into agreements.

Art. 9 requires a continuous, iterative risk management system that identifies, estimates, evaluates, and mitigates risks throughout the lifecycle, informed by post-market monitoring data under Art. 72. AI Risk Management applies structured processes to identify, evaluate, mitigate, and track AI risks across the lifecycle.

Art. 15(5) requires technical solutions for AI-specific vulnerabilities and Art. 9(2) requires continuous identification and treatment of risks. Cybersecurity Risk Management continuously evaluates threats, vulnerabilities, and exposure across systems and AI workloads.

Art. 73 requires providers to report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority within 15 days, 10 days for death, and 2 days for widespread infringement or critical infrastructure disruption, Art. 20(2) requires informing authorities of non-conformity, and Art. 55(1)(c) requires systemic-risk GPAI providers to report to the AI Office. Regulatory Reporting meets these notification obligations in time and content.

Art. 20 requires the provider to decide on corrective actions, withdrawal, disabling, or recall of a non-conforming system, which under the Art. 17(1)(m) accountability framework is a management decision. Top Management provides the executive briefings that inform those decisions. Partial alignment: the Act does not address internal escalation.

Art. 73 requires reporting of serious incidents within short time limits, followed by investigation and risk assessment, and Art. 20 requires immediate corrective action. Incident Response Team maintains the synchronised internal communication needed to meet those deadlines. Partial alignment: the Act sets outcomes, not team structure.

Art. 50 requires public-facing disclosure that content is AI-generated or that a person is interacting with AI, Art. 20(2) requires informing distributors, deployers, and importers of non-conformity, and Art. 53(1)(d) requires a public summary of GPAI training content. Public Updates / Disclosures manages approved public communications that balance transparency and risk.

Art. 43(2) allows conformity assessment based on internal control under Annex VI, which requires the provider to verify that the QMS complies with Art. 17 and that the technical documentation and design meet the requirements. Internal Audit provides the independent assurance over those controls that internal-control conformity assessment presumes.

Art. 9(6) to (8) require high-risk systems to be tested to identify the most appropriate risk management measures, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, at any point in development and before placing on the market, Art. 17(1)(d) requires test procedures, and Art. 60 governs real-world testing. Testing plans and executes functional, security, reliability, and safety tests of systems and AI components.

Art. 49 requires providers and public-authority deployers to register high-risk systems in the EU database under Art. 71 before placing on the market or putting into service, and Art. 26 obligations attach to each deployed high-risk system. AI System Inventory maintains the authoritative inventory of AI systems and components that registration and per-system compliance depend on.

Art. 10(2) requires documentation of data collection processes, origin of data, and preparation operations, and Annex IV(2)(d) requires description of training methodologies and datasets including provenance, scope, and main characteristics. Data Mapping documents end-to-end data flows including AI training and inference.

Art. 27 requires deployers of certain high-risk systems to assess the impact on fundamental rights, including affected persons, risks of harm, oversight measures, and mitigations, and Art. 9(9) requires consideration of impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups. AI Impacts identifies potential impacts on individuals, groups, and society and integrates mitigations.

Art. 9(2)(a) and (b) require identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights from intended use and foreseeable misuse, and Art. 55(1)(b) requires identification of systemic risks for GPAI. Risk Identification identifies risks spanning cyber, privacy, safety, ethics, and AI trust for consistent analysis.

Art. 25(4) requires written agreements with suppliers of AI systems, tools, services, components, or processes used in high-risk systems, and Art. 53 sets obligations that downstream providers rely on from GPAI providers. Supply Chain Risk identifies and manages the risks from suppliers of software, models, datasets, and cloud services.

Art. 9(8) requires testing against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds appropriate to the intended purpose, Art. 9(5) requires residual risk to be acceptable, Art. 14(4)(a) requires oversight persons to detect anomalies and unexpected performance, and Art. 15(3) requires declared accuracy levels and metrics. AI Operational Thresholds defines the measurable thresholds for performance, fairness, drift, and safety with rollback and human-in-the-loop criteria.

Art. 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment whenever a high-risk system is substantially modified, unless pre-determined changes were assessed in advance, and Art. 25(1) makes anyone who makes a substantial modification or changes the intended purpose a provider. Change Management ensures changes to systems, datasets, models, and configurations are risk-assessed, approved, and auditable.

Art. 9(2) requires risk management across the entire lifecycle, Art. 17(1)(b) to (d) require documented design, development, verification, and validation procedures, Art. 72 requires post-market monitoring, and Art. 18 requires documentation to be kept for 10 years. AI System Lifecycle institutionalises an AI SDLC embedding governance and TEVV from design to decommissioning.

Art. 10(2)(f) and (g) require examination of possible biases likely to affect health, safety, or fundamental rights and measures to detect, prevent, and mitigate them, Art. 14(4)(b) requires awareness of automation bias, and Art. 15(4) requires measures against feedback loops. Bias detects and reduces unjustified bias across the lifecycle and documents residual risks.

Art. 15(1) requires high-risk systems to achieve an appropriate level of robustness and perform consistently throughout the lifecycle, and Art. 15(4) requires resilience to errors, faults, and inconsistencies in the environment through redundancy, backup, and fail-safe plans. Robustness ensures models withstand distribution shift and adversarial conditions with predictable fail-safe behaviour.

Art. 13 requires operation to be sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret output, with instructions for use covering capabilities, limitations, and known risks, Art. 14(4)(c) requires that oversight persons can correctly interpret output, and Art. 86 gives affected persons a right to an explanation. Explainability provides audience-appropriate transparency and interpretability and discloses limits.

Art. 10(2) requires documented data provenance, preparation, and bias examination, Art. 10(3) requires datasets to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and as free of errors as possible, and Art. 53(1)(c) and (d) require copyright compliance and a training-content summary for GPAI. Datasets & Tagging protects training and inference data integrity and lawful use through provenance, licensing, and sensitivity labelling.

Art. 15(5) requires technical solutions that prevent, detect, respond to, resolve, and control attacks exploiting AI-specific vulnerabilities, naming data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, model evasion, and confidentiality attacks, and Art. 55(1)(d) requires cybersecurity protection for systemic-risk GPAI. AI-Specific Attack Vectors mitigates prompt injection, poisoning, model theft, jailbreaks, and abuse.

Art. 4 requires providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and others operating AI on their behalf, Art. 26(2) requires oversight persons to have the necessary competence and training, and Art. 14(5) requires remote biometric identification results to be separately verified by at least two competent persons. AI Training educates stakeholders on ethical, secure, and responsible AI development and use.

Art. 10(5) requires that processing of special-category data for bias detection use technical limitations on re-use, security and privacy-preserving measures such as pseudonymisation, access controls, and deletion once bias correction is complete, and Art. 59 sets similar safeguards for sandboxes. Privacy Controls embeds privacy-enhancing technologies and governance in systems that process personal data.

Art. 15(5) requires that cybersecurity measures be built into the system design, and Art. 17(1)(b) and (c) require documented design control, development, quality control, and quality assurance techniques. Secure Development integrates security and AI-specific assurance into the SDLC from design through release.

Art. 73 requires providers to report serious incidents, investigate them, perform a risk assessment, and take corrective action, Art. 20 requires corrective actions for non-conforming systems, and Art. 26(5) requires deployers to inform providers and authorities. Incident Response: AI ensures coordinated response to AI incidents such as harmful outputs, data leakage, or unauthorised model behaviour.

Art. 9(2)(c) requires evaluation of risks emerging from post-market monitoring data, Art. 72(2) requires that data to be analysed to evaluate continuous compliance, and Art. 20 requires corrective actions after non-conformity. Incident Lessons Learned ensures each incident results in measurable learning and control enhancement.

Art. 43 requires conformity assessment of high-risk systems, with notified-body assessment of the QMS and technical documentation under Annex VII for certain systems, and Art. 44 governs the resulting certificates. External Audit: AI Audit obtains independent assurance over AI governance and risk controls, including lifecycle evidence.

Art. 85 gives any person the right to lodge a complaint with a market surveillance authority, Art. 87 applies the Whistleblower Directive to reports of infringements, and Art. 86 gives a right to explanation of decisions. Reporting Channels provides safe and responsive channels for employees, customers, and users to report risks, incidents, or ethical concerns.

Art. 9(6) to (8) require testing to determine that the system performs consistently for its intended purpose, Art. 15 requires appropriate and declared levels of accuracy and robustness, and Art. 55(1)(a) requires model evaluation including adversarial testing for systemic-risk GPAI. Evaluation evaluates model and system performance, safety, and harms across realistic operating contexts.

Art. 17(1)(b) requires design verification techniques within the QMS, and Annex VI(3) requires the provider to verify that the system meets the requirements of Section 2 of Chapter III. Verification confirms that implemented systems meet stated requirements and that controls operate as designed.

Art. 9(6) requires testing to ensure consistent performance for the intended purpose, Art. 17(1)(d) requires validation procedures during and after development, and Art. 60 allows real-world testing under specified conditions. Validation confirms the system as built and operated achieves its intended use for target users without unacceptable risk.
